query: For automotive exhaust catalysts, what single intervention could improve catalytic activity and durability while reducing platinum-group-metal consumption? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing nitrogen into the synthesis of a high‐entropy alloy catalyst to generate multiple metal–nitrogen bonds and leverage multicomponent mixing to stabilize a Pt‐rich shell will simultaneously boost catalytic oxidation activity and durability for automotive exhaust reactions while allowing for reduced platinum-group-metal usage.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of a multi‐principal element HEA (e.g., containing Co, Pd, Fe, Ni, Cu, etc.) with conventional Pt loading deposited on them, produced without any nitrogen doping.
generation.intervention: Integrate nitrogen doping during the synthesis (for example by a controlled thermal annealing in an NH3 atmosphere) to form robust metal–nitrogen bonds within the HEA core and at the interface with a deliberately engineered Pt‐rich shell.
generation.conditions: The catalyst is evaluated under high-temperature, oxidative conditions typical of automotive exhaust systems with thermal cycling and exposure to exhaust gas components.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of multiple metal–nitrogen bonds in the HEA structure creates a stabilized, electronically optimized Pt-rich shell, anchoring atomically dispersed Pt species and preventing their agglomeration or dissolution.
generation.mechanism: Nitrogen incorporation is expected to create strong M–N bonds that modulate the electronic structure of the Pt sites, reducing poisoning by adsorbed species and enhancing oxidation kinetics. At the same time, the high configurational entropy (multicomponent mixing) of the HEA imparts excellent thermal stability, thereby improving durability under harsh exhaust conditions while enabling lower overall PGM loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventional Pt/C or non‐N-doped Pt–HEA catalysts, the N-doped HEA catalyst should exhibit a notably lower light-off temperature (an expected reduction of approximately 20–30%), enhanced mass activity and sustained performance over extended thermal cycling, and allow a reduction in Pt loading (e.g., up to 50% lower PGM consumption) while maintaining or improving catalytic performance.
generation.baseline: Automotive exhaust catalysts currently based on conventional Pt/C or Pt/alloy catalysts on standard supports without nitrogen doping.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected under high-temperature, oxidizing conditions found in real automotive exhaust systems; improvements may not manifest under milder conditions or if the nitrogen doping does not remain stable during prolonged high-temperature operation.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements (in terms of activity, durability, and Pt consumption reduction) are uncertain until validated experimentally; additionally, the long-term thermal stability of the nitrogen-modified structures under real-world conditions needs to be confirmed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two catalyst samples: one HEA-based catalyst with a Pt-rich shell synthesized under an NH3 atmosphere (to incorporate nitrogen doping) and one identical control synthesized in an inert atmosphere. Incorporate both catalysts into a laboratory-scale diesel oxidation reactor setup. Subject them to standard automotive exhaust simulation testing, including light-off temperature measurement for CO oxidation, extended thermal cycling/durability tests, and assessments of Pt leaching via ICP-MS.
measurements: Light-off temperature (e.g., T50 for CO oxidation)
Mass activity (current per mg of Pt) at set temperatures
Durability metrics (activity retention or voltage shift after defined thermal cycles)
Quantification of Pt content before and after testing (to evaluate PGM consumption and leaching)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nitrogen-doped HEA catalyst does not demonstrate at least a 20% improvement in light-off temperature, significantly enhanced mass activity and durability (e.g., less than 10% degradation after prolonged testing), and measurable reduction in Pt usage compared to the control, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: We successfully synthesized the N–Pt/HEA catalyst with a Pt-rich shell and a high entropy alloy PtCoFeNiCu core with multiple M–N bonds via a facile thermal annealing process and an acid-etching de-alloying strategy. The N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst possesses a unique structure and electrochemical stability, resulting in excellent long-term durability under HDV conditions. Detailed studies on atomic structure utilizing in situ synchrotron XRD and XAS, coupled with HAADF-STEM/EDS and DFT calculations, allowed the elucidation of influencing factors on the catalytic properties and performance of the novel catalyst. The high performance of N–Pt/HEA/C originates from the combined effect of high entropy, multiple M-N bonds, and a Pt-rich shell. In addition to the enhancement of corrosion resistance, the M–N bonds through N-doping can boost the activity and durability of the electrocatalyst by the distortion effect in the core structure. The synergy between the three factors further endows the N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst to outperform the state-of-the-art Pt/C electrocatalysts and most binary/ternary Pt-based catalysts for the ORR. AbstractThe modification of Pt surfaces with organic compounds like melamine enhances oxygen reduction reaction activity and catalyst durability. Through first-principles free energy calculations utilizing thermodynamic integration and finite-temperature molecular dynamics, enhanced by machine learning force fields for efficient sampling of nanosecond-scale interfacial water fluctuations and incorporating corrections to accurately reproduce first-principles free energies, we demonstrate that melamine destabilizes OH adsorbates, facilitating their removal and enhancing catalytic activity. Unlike alloys, where OH destabilization is driven by changes in electronic structure and surface strain, melamine disrupts hydrogen bonding between OH and interfacial water. Structural and vibrational analyses reveal that melamine alters the water solvation structure, which is evident in modified radial distribution functions and a blue shift in the O–H stretching vibrations. These findings indicate that manipulating interfacial solvation with organic compounds could be a promising approach to enhance catalytic activity without compromising durability.
